It was just a website

This is a massive understatement. It's not just one page, or a few pages thrown together. It's an entire health insurance exchange infrastructure.

The website has to serve residents of 36 states that don't manage their own exchanges. User have to be able to create accounts, browse and compare providers, and purchase insurance from the website. The translates to a massive amount of integrations with health care providers, security systems and payment processing systems. Also keep in mind that citizens were legally obligated to have healthcare by a certain date, and this is the website that was supposed to facilitate the process for a ton of people.

That said, the entire fiasco can be summarized by saying, "the administration did not provide effective planning or oversight practices."

The government contracted the development and testing work out to a few groups. Development was started without having a finalized plan and testing seems to have been essentially non-existent. Delivery dates during development were consistently unmet and a review of the process seems to indicate that, of what little testing was done, the testing groups had little ability to delay development (that is, major issues were "swept under the rug").

When finally launching, the expectation was that they would need to handle 50,000 to 60,000 simultaneous users. Contractors preformed a stress test 1 day before "go-live" and found that the site became too slow with only 1,100 simultaneous users. They went live the next day, and were hit with 250,000 simultaneous users. In the first 4 days, the site had 8.1 million unique visitors.

Basically, this was a huge task and it was poorly developed and tested. Even if it had been done well from the start, something this critical needed more time. They've since made substantial improvements to the website, clearing up most of the problems that lead to the failed launch.

Here's a little more of a rundown on how users were supposed to experience the website and the problems encountered at launch:

  1. Front page: pick state and create account
    • Problem: user had to create an account first before being able to compare providers. When 250,000 people try to do that, the system breaks.
  2. Registration: the actual account creation
    • Problem: the integration between some of the systems wasn't working correctly, so many accounts failed to create
  3. Proof of Identity: registration had to pass verification tool and verification by Experian
  4. Eligibility: customer data is sent to a "data hub" that contacts dozens of federal and state agencies, and verifies income with Equifax
    • Problem : step 3 and 4 require the data communication between these different system all be working, but there were many issues with that.
  5. Shop for plan: now assuming you made it though step 4, you'd be fortunate enough to be able to finally browse for a plan, unless...
    • Problem: many users that were eligible for subsidies or Medicaid were incorrectly determined as not-eligible in step 4.
  6. Insurance translation: a purchase form with plan information has to get set to the "data hub" again to be converted into an electronic format that insurance companies can receive
  7. Insurance enrollment: Insurer gets report of every person that enrolled that day
    • Problem: the reports (known as "834s") can be very confusing and have a lot of duplicate information, leading to insurance companies that are, no joke, unsure of who their new customers really are.
  8. Coverage: lucky enough to get through step 7, and you're insurer actually has a record of everything, then you're covered!
    • Problem: if you're insurer doesn't think you're a customer, your not really covered, but you have no way of immediately knowing that.
